21418-the-eugenic-marriage-volume-4-of-4:
Volume four of W. Grant Hague's The Eugenic Marriage, issued in 1913, closes his guide to better living and better babies. Hague was a New York doctor trained at Columbia's College of Physicians and Surgeons. He wrote in the name of eugenics, then a much-praised new science.

The pages give rules for the care of young children in the home. Hague warns against letting babies crawl on cold floors, where draughts run low. Beds, sofas, or raised boards are urged for play instead. Modern readers will read the book as a record of its age, since eugenics is now rejected and condemned.
2836-abraham-lincoln-and-the-union-a-chr:
Nathaniel Stephenson wrote this short history of Abraham Lincoln and the Union for the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1918. The volume covers the Civil War years from Lincoln's side, following the president, his cabinet, and the northern public through secession, compromise efforts, and war. Stephenson warns that no brief book can settle every dispute about the era.

The narrative stresses the political work of holding the North together, including figures such as Crittenden and Everett and the search for a settlement that might save the Union. Lincoln stands at the center as a manager of competing pressures rather than a distant hero. The book suits readers who want a compact, readable account of the embattled North.
5641-man-or-matter-introduction-to-a-spi:
Ernst Lehrs wrote Man or Matter as an introduction to a spiritual understanding of nature, based on Goethe's method of training observation and thought. The book opens with the author's search for a way to extend scientific understanding, and a meeting with Rudolf Steiner and the work arising from his teachings. Later chapters diagnose modern science's self-restriction to one-eyed, colorblind observation.

Lehrs argues that such observation leaves no true conception of force, and treats thought as both sole reality and pure non-entity for the modern spectator. Goetheanism, dynamics, levity, and counter-space follow. Readers get a thoughtful, demanding work of Goethean science, for readers open to spirit in nature.
5712-sculpture-of-the-exposition-palaces:
Juliet James describes the sculpture of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco, palace by palace and court by court. Dedicated to A Stirling Calder, who managed the execution of the sculpture, the notes honor the vast body of sculptors and their workers whose figures crowned the fair. James treats statues, groups, and fountains as a single planned decoration, not as isolated ornaments.

Readers gain a guided walk through a vanished fairground, learning what each figure meant and how it fit its building. The book suits lovers of public art, World's Fair history, and early twentieth-century American sculpture. It preserves in words a display meant to last only a season, and it helps modern readers picture the exposition's grandeur.
6875-france-and-england-in-north-america:
Francis Parkman centers this fifth part of his history on Count Frontenac, the governor who stood for the French crown in the New World under Louis XIV. The preface calls him the most striking man ever to hold that post, a leader who grew with each crisis after a most unpromising start. His career runs through petty quarrels and through clashes that decided which nation would hold the continent.

Parkman follows Frontenac through war, rivalry, and rule in New France, showing how a system built on central command met a foe stronger in numbers. The volume looks back from a time when that old contest for North America had long been settled, and it weighs what one forceful governor could and could not do.
6933-france-and-england-in-north-america:
Francis Parkman devotes the second part of his history to the French Jesuits in North America in the seventeenth century. His preface calls their efforts to convert the Indians among the most striking passages of history, full of dramatic and philosophic interest. Their work bore hard on the political fate of America and on the story of its native peoples, yet had long lain in obscurity.

While infant English colonies still clung feebly to the Atlantic shore, events ominous for their future moved in the heart of the continent, unknown to them. Parkman follows the missionaries into that interior world, where faith, empire, and native nations met. The volume is both mission history and a prelude to the contest for a continent.
7069-expositions-of-holy-scripture-genes:
Alexander MacLaren expounds Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers in this volume of Holy Scripture expositions. The Genesis contents open with the vision of creation, how sin came in, and Eden lost and restored. The growth and power of sin, what crouches at the door, and with, before, after trace a devout life. The course and crown of such a life and the saint among sinners follow.

Clear shining after rain, the sign for man and remembrancer for God, and an example of faith lead to Abram going forth and coming in as a man of faith. Life in Canaan and the importance of a choice close the opening set. MacLaren preaches text by text, drawing doctrine and daily conduct from each passage with plain, earnest care.
abraham-lincoln-and-the-union-a-chronicl:
Nathaniel W. Stephenson writes a brief chronicle of Lincoln and the Union as volume 29 of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1918, with Allen Johnson as series editor. His preface cuts the task to two questions: why was there a war, and why did the Lincoln government succeed?

Chapters move from the party of political evasion through secession and war to Lincoln himself, his rule, his treasury secretary, northern life during the war, and the vote of 1864. Stephenson writes clear narrative history for general readers, with Lincoln's career as the spine. The book appeared while another war raged, and its interest in national unity has a wartime edge.

expositions-of-holy-scripture-genesis-ex:
Alexander Maclaren's Expositions of Holy Scripture: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers offers sermon-like expositions of the first four books of the Bible. Maclaren, a celebrated Baptist preacher, treats each passage as a text for devotional reflection rather than as a problem for scholars alone.

Genesis expositions include The Vision of Creation, How Sin Came In, Eden Lost and Restored, The Growth and Power of Sin, and God's Covenant with Abram. Later volumes in the series carry the method through Exodus, Leviticus and Numbers. Readers seeking Victorian evangelical preaching at its most thoughtful will find Maclaren clear, warm and richly illustrative.
france-and-england-in-north-america-part:
Francis Parkman's The Jesuits in North America in the Seventeenth Century is the second part of his France and England in North America series. Parkman calls the early French Jesuits' efforts to convert the Indians among the most striking passages of history, full of dramatic and philosophic interest.

While England's infant colonies still clung feebly to the Atlantic shore, events ominous to their future were unfolding in the heart of the continent. Parkman draws on the Jesuit Relations and other sources to follow missionaries among the Hurons and their neighbours. Readers will find here the classic account of the missions, their heroism, their politics, and their entanglement with the fate of New France.

Francis Parkman's Count Frontenac and New France Under Louis XIV is the fifth part of his France and England in North America series. Parkman presents Frontenac as France's most remarkable representative in the New World, growing with every emergency and rising equal to every crisis.

The narrative groups itself around Frontenac's governorship, his struggles with rivals and with the English colonies, and his defence of New France. Parkman writes with the vivid, dramatic power that made his histories famous, while keeping close to documents and to the ground itself. Readers of Canadian and colonial American history will find Frontenac a commanding centre for a turbulent age.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Pre-Assassinati: Pre-assassination FBI wiretapping: the title of this declassified US government document, via the Internet Archive. The Norris name hints at the subject, but the catalog gives no date, no case detail. Text not publicly located. A suggestive title, thinly documented.
man-or-matter-introduction-to-a-spiritua:
Man or Matter introduces a spiritual way of understanding nature. Ernst Lehrs, a doctor of philosophy, built it on Goethe's method. Goethe trained observation and thought together, and Lehrs follows him. An early chapter tells of Lehrs's meeting with Rudolf Steiner.

Lehrs charges modern science with one-eyed, color-blind observation. It lacks, he says, a true conception of force. Descartes and Hume come in for sharp criticism. Electricity, man's competitor in modern life, gets long attention. The book asks readers to seek the soul of nature, not just its shell. It speaks to students of Goethe and of Steiner alike.
nasa-tm-19680009741-flight-vibration-dat:
Arney N. Munson, of the Test and Evaluation Division at Goddard Space Flight Center, compiled this final report in December 1967. It presents flight vibration data from the Astrobee 1500 sounding rocket, on NASA flight 16.02. Sounding rockets shake hard at launch, and payload builders need real records of how rough the ride was.

Three channels of high-frequency vibration data came from crystal accelerometers mounted on the payload support structure. Strong transient responses struck at first and second stage ignition, which is typical, and again just after first stage burnout. That later response is blamed on the anomalous release of the clam-shell heat shield. Random vibration stayed low through the transonic and maximum pressure stretches. About twenty seconds after second stage burnout, the payload began rigid body coning motions. The likely cause was the spinning fiberglass motor case unwrapping under high temperatures.
nasa-tm-19680021941-future-aspects-of-su:
Robert Jon Pawlak of NASA's Electronics Research Center in Cambridge outlines future supersonic transport navigation in this paper. Supersonic airliners need navigation, guidance, and control electronics that work as one system. Requirements studies were complete, and a five-year research plan had been drawn up when he wrote.

The goal is a hybrid avionics system that uses each navigation method where it works best. Tasks under way included a passive navigation and traffic control satellite system. Other work targeted better all-weather landing using inertial data. Strapdown sensor redundancy, fuel-optimum climb paths, and laser gyro research also feature. Pawlak presents study results, the long-range plan, and current progress.
sculpture-of-the-exposition-palaces-and-:
Juliet James wrote these notes on the statues placed around the palaces and courts of the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco. She dedicates the book to A. Stirling Calder, who directed the carving work, and to the many sculptors and workmen behind it.

James praises the fair's art as sincere, skilled, and truly American in spirit. She argues that American carving came of age after the Centennial fair of 1876. Her notes guide a fair visitor statue by statue, giving lay readers a way to judge work they might else walk past without a second look.
st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-girls-:
St. Nicholas, Volume V, Number 3, for January 1878, under an 1877 copyright of Scribner and Co., opens with The Ravens and the Angels, a story of the Middle Ages. Its author is named only as the author of Chronicles of the Schönberg-Cotta Family. A front picture shows two ways of carrying the mail. The tale starts in an old city where folk called the cathedral, and thought it, the house of God.

Since the cathedral was the Father's house for all, the poor might nestle close to its gates. When Berthold the stone-carver died, his young wife Magdalis and her two small children, Gottlieb and Lenichen, were let to live in a little wooden shed by the great west gate. Inside, choir song rolled night and day. Outside rose the sighs of a sad woman and the cries of children her toil could scarce feed with bread.

St. Nicholas, Volume V, Number 12, dates to October 1878. Scribner and Co. held its copyright. Edith Hawkins opens it with The Violin Village. A front picture shows the noon encampment. Mittenwald lies on the borders of the Tyrol. Lofty mountains shut the quaint village in. Its folk make stringed instruments for a living. On fine days the gardens blossom in an odd way.

Zithers and guitars hang drying on lines like clothes. Violins by the hundreds join them there. One August morning at five, a lad leaves a gabled house. Stephan is the village goatherd. He is not more than twelve years old. Green trims his gray suit of coarse cloth. His knees and feet are bare. A whip and a small brass horn hang at his shoulder. Black cock's feathers crown his high felt hat.
the-eugenic-marriage-volume-1-of-4-a-per: W. Grant Hague's The Eugenic Marriage, volume one of four, styles itself a personal guide to the new science of better living and better babies. Hague, of Columbia's College of Physicians and Surgeons, saw the set printed at New York in 1916. Only the title matter and a long index for all four volumes are present here. None of Hague's counsel appears in these pages.
the-fugitive-slave-law-and-its-victims-a:
The Fugitive Slave Law and Its Victims is tract number eighteen of the American Anti-Slavery Society, printed at New York in 1856. It opens with the law's birth and a plain summary of its ten parts.

The tract notes that Congress passed the law in September 1850 and President Millard Fillmore signed it on September 18. It calls the act, in the words of a New York paper, an act for the encouragement of kidnapping. Federal officers were bound to help seize folk claimed as runaways, with no jury and no voice for the accused. Case by case, the tract then names the law's victims.
